blocks.x: SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION
Jazz Oral History Project
J.C. Johnson
Reel 1
Interviewed by Sunna Rasch (December 1978)
Washington, D.C.
March, 1980

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5895
P R O C E E D I N G S
MS. RASCH: This tape was made for the Smithsonian's Oral History Project. I'm Sunna Rasch of Periwinkle Productions on the J.C. Johnson project.

The following tapes contain conversations between J.C. and me. The first interview was taken in the late Fall of 1978; J.C. had just come out of Doctors Hospital and was feeling quite fit at the time, and the tone reflects his vigor which was, unfortunately, not to last for too long.
And so the first tape begins:
Good afternoon to you, Sunna.
I'm so delighted to be with you, J.C., and particularly so today, because the Smithsonian, as you know, has commissioned an Oral History project on the life and times of J.C. Johnson.
Well, the Smithsonian is one of the greatest.
So J.C., I thought maybe -- we've got so many years -- how old are you, first of all?
Well, do you really want my true age?
Well, I know you look very young.
I mean, but do you want the real McCoy?
Sure do.
Well, it's past 82.
Past 82?
Past 82, and I'm very happy about that, too.
Me, too, and you look about 72!
Oh, go on, you're something, you know? You make people feel good!
No, it's the truth, it's really the truth. You've seen a lot in the world, and you've had a big impact on the jazz movement in our country, but I'd like to ask you a couple of questions, first.
Go right ahead, go right ahead.
Because I'd like to know, were you an only child ...
Yes.
You were an only child. Well, you know, when they made you, they threw away the pattern.
Right.
You agree?
And threw away my father on top of it. I had very much of him.
Really?
No, my mother had to do it all.
Well, it's not too much different
from today, when these fathers get so busy they don't make time for their kids.
Yes, yes.
You know? It works at both ends of the poles, you know?
Yes, yeah.
All right, well anyway, I'd like to hear about your mother, because she sounds like a wonderful person.

She was the greatest -- positively the greatest. She always said to me if you're going to be anything, try to be good, and try to be the best. Don't just be along with the rest, she said just be the best -- at whatever you do, do it excellently.

This desire for excellence that she ingrained in you at such an early age paid off because I've known you for quite some time now, Jay, and I just see in everything you do is this desire for excellence; there is no half way about it.
And that's a wonderful gift. Now was it she who influenced you to take the piano, or did you play another instrument first?
No. She asked me if I'd like the piano, she knew that I was going next door down the street to people who had a piano because we didn't have one; we

couldn't afford one, and so she asked if I liked it and I said yes, and she said 'Well, every opportunity that you get, play it. I'm sorry I can't give you lessons right now, but I'm doing the best I can right now.'
Uh huh.
So I had to do the best I could and get what I could wherever I could get it.
Did you take lessons?
I took lessons from Professor Lee.
Uh huh.
But my money ran out fast! (Laughs)
So --
So I had to do without the rest of the lessons, and work my way up into a dither, I might say, where I got to the point where I could go for myself.

You know, Jay, I wonder who -- aside from your mother and Professor Lee -- in those years of growing up, when did you first know that you wanted music, professionally, that that's where you wanted to dedicate your excellence, and who influenced you the most?

Well, I was much too young to really know, because when you're real young, all you know is that you would like to play, and in playing, you were having pleasure, and you were enjoying what you were doing -- so the next step was for me to get into the groove where I could
do a little something that I liked to do.
Uh huh.
So a bunch of us fellows down the road a piece, I might say, because living the way I did, why, you had to belong to a group or you couldn't navigate, you see?
Uh huh. And it hasn't changed!

Not a bit. If you didn't belong to a gang, you didn't move -- so I belonged to the gang, and one wanted one thing and one another. We all wanted different things. I was the only one in there who wanted music.
So you know, who might you say influenced you?

Well, the person who influenced me the most was a person - foreign, I might say, foreign to the profession, because I liked music that I could hear; I had to hear it to enjoy it, and the people who were playing it, not necessarily for me, but for the world, weren't the ones who made it for me.
You weren't really relating to it?
No, I wasn't relating to them. Because they played such beautiful and intricate material; I would never latch on to it. It wasn't ...
Could you name like a song ...
Oh, Scott Joplin, and years later, a

bunch of us songwriters had a meeting, in Scott Joplin's home in New York, and his wife was still living and a bunch of us songwriters met in her home, which I imagine we contributed to, Lottie Joplin, and well, so many of us -- honest to goodness, you wouldn't know what to do with the rest of us.
Oh? Do you remember, we were talking a long time ago, you were telling me about the first time you hear Herbie Miller's songs?
Yes.
Do you remember what that song was? You said you didn't understand it.
No, I didn't understand it.

But you said something about it blew out of the ground ... do you remember what that song was? Maybe I've got a note on it somewhere; I'll have to go back and find it, but I just thought you might pull it out of the top of your head.
Yes, yes.
Right now you go back an awful long time to remember.
That was a long time ago.
All right, when did you start playing professionally? I mean, who gave you your first paid job? Your first gig, your first real honest to goodness paycheck job?

Oh, that would be doggone just next to impossible for me to tell you who gave me my first pennies for playing because I never cared about playing for money, and I never cared about being a pianist, to tell you the truth.
I wanted to be just a guy who wrote little tunes, and things like that -- I wanted to write something, I wanted to compose.
Uh huh. Fine. All right. I have to go back, you know, I have missed your playing so much, J.C. I just hope that one of these days, we'll make up for lost time.
Oh, yes ...
But what was the first song that you wrote, that you composed?
The first song that I wrote and composed was 'You Can't Do What My Last Man Did'.
How old were you?
Oh, my gosh --how old is the song is the question!
Oh, all right.
I was 102, but the song was ...
Oh, but you were just a young kid, right?
Of course -- just getting ready. And Ethel Waters was the one who did that song, who made it and
did the first recording of 'You Can't Do What My Last Man Did'. Who recorded it? Do you remember?
She did -- Ethel Waters.
No, but what -- do you remember what label?
Oh ... Black Swan.
Uh huh.
Black Swan.
How did you meet Ethel Waters?
She recorded it and I played for her.
Yes, I know -- but did you meet her before she sang that song?
Oh, yes, yes.
How?

We were friends -- we were friends long before she sang the song because just ordinary social strides among us -- I knew her so well and she knew me, and friends of hers and friends of mine, we were just socially okay, and so when it came to her recording, she was made to order for it.
But did you write it with her in mind, as singing it -- was it one of those things?
No, I didn't -- but after it was written, after I wrote it, why, I thought she was the
best prospect for it.

Uh huh. Did you ever write for certain people? In other words, did somebody stimulate your creativity in that respect, you know; say, oh, well -- Bessie Smith -- did you know Bessie Smith before you wrote "Empty Bed Blues"?

Yes, yes, I did -- I knew Bessie Smith before that because of the fact that Porter Granger introduced me to her. He said there was somebody I wanted you to meet, and so he introduced me to Bessie. And it wasn't very long after that that I wrote "Empty Bed Blues."
Do you know what Herbie Harper told me?
No.
He told me that you used to escort Lena Horne home from the Cotton Club to keep the wolves away!
Yes.
Tell me about that.

Yes, well Claude Hopkins was part of that brigade -- Claude and myself, we -- Claude and me, we used to take her home to keep the wolves away, because there were plenty of them looking -- and at her age, she was young and one of the prettiest gals you would ever want to see.
She's still a beauty.
Isn't she?
Yes.
And we used to -- she probably wouldn't even remember, so, but we used to -- Claude and I -- we used to run the guns on them, keep the cats away.
I guarantee you that she remembers, and well!
I wonder.
Oh, sure.
You know, it would be great thing to know if she does remember, it would be a wonderful thing to hook that up with this.
I tell you what -- I think I'll drop her a note; how about that? Why not, right?
Yes.
Got to have a good old reunion down here.

We loved her, we -- she was part of us and we were part of her, and we wanted to see that nothing happened to her. Claude is still around, I think, and we used to run the guns on her. And Lena's still living, and if she is still living, she's as pretty as she ever was, I might say.
Yes, she sure is. Now, J.C., I wonder -- of all the people that you've worked with, and that

runs a large gamut of both, you know, composers -- people like Fats, singers, like Lena Horne and Bessie Smith and Ethel Waters and all these others -- and just musicians, just the men that took this music and just breathed life into it ...
Yes?
Who stands out in your mind the most? I mean, whom do you really hold dear as a personal kind of association, and whom do you look at as this was a genius, this was a genius, and we worked together?
Fats Waller.
Fats. You know, I know three of your songs are in his 'Ain't Misbehaving' on Broadway right now.
Yes.

And I had an old flyer from the Manhattan Theatre Club when they did the show first, before they brought it to Broadway, and they advertised it by saying, "The joint is jumpin'" and I looked and I said, "That's JC's song!"
Oh, yes.
Now how did you get to meet Fats and what was he like?
Well, he was 19 years old when I met him, only a kid.
Well, how old were you?
Well, I'm a little older than that.
No, but I mean was there -- how old would Fats be if he were living, do you think?
Oh, he was in his forties when he died; he died very young, you know -- very, very young. But Fats came along at a time -- Fats lived very fast.
I was gonna say, he did a lot of living in that short time.
Yes, yes; Fats lived fast -- and I have on the back of an album something that Fats took his pen to and he wrote, 'To my best friend, J.C. Johnson'.
I believe that.

I've got that. Now, how do you become the best friend of Fats Waller with all the people in the world that he knows, and all the friends that he has? How do you become his best friend, 'to my only and best friend', and that's what he said I was to him.
Well, that's because you're you.
And his wife told me when he died, you must be his head pall bearer because I know that would please him, to have you at that spot, because he loved you very dearly.
JC, there are so few people in this world with integrity, the great combination of integrity and talent.
Yes, yes.
And he knew it when he saw it. Now, when you first met him, and he was 19 -- what was he like? What was he like?
Just a youngster full of vim, vigor and wigor! Just full of everything that you have at 19 years old!
I know, I know.
And he was full of it, and big enough to have a lot of it.
Right, right.
So, oh, golly -- when Fats came in, everybody had to move over, because the room got smaller.
Ha!

So he was the most wonderful guy -- I don't know of anyone in my life that publishes on Broadway would do what they did with Fats. Fats would sell the same songs to six publishers, and not one of those publishers would ever get angry with Fats.
I guess you couldn't.
You just couldn't. He was under your skin and he stayed there. He lived under your skin.
Oh, that's a nice way to put it.
That's right, and he was just so wonderful because you would ask Fats for a song one day, maybe two weeks later, he'd say, 'Take it, take it.' They all got
paid for what they did. They enjoyed it and they loved him, they loved him -- I never saw a guy yet who held a spot that he held in the hearts of those tough guys down Broadway. But he was one.
Uh huh. And you held the spot in his heart.
Yes.
All right now, do you remember how you first met him? You know, do you remember when the situation was? And I know that's going back a long time, of course ...
Yeah, that's quite a ways back.
Is that something you've got to think about?
Well, it's just one of those things you grow up together, and you know how you grow up together, there's just no way of telling how you got together. All it is is that you were there.
Just a case of timing, really.
That's it.
Right. Well, was it Chicago or New York?
New York.
It was New York.
Yes.
All right.
I don't think Fats liked much of Chicago. I was out here since, well, 19 --
Nineteen what?
Nineteen uh uh!
(Laughter)
I'll be darned. That's great. Perfect.

So Fats was here already, so we got together -- Hey, Fats! Hey there. And it started, you know, it was just one of those things, and he was a genius. The man could do more with the keys on the board than anyone I ever knew in my life.
How did you work together, you know, as collaborators -- how did that work? Could you kind of describe it?
Well, see, Fats would play something if he had it, if he had a tune, he'd say, 'Dig this!' and he'd play the tune. Well, you got to be fast enough to write the lyrics.
And you would just feel it. It was a real partnership.
That's right. And so you would write it with Fats; he would play it over and you would write it. He'd say, 'Play the last part again,' And you'd play it over, and that was it.
And that would just spire and tie together.
That's right.
Did you ever prefer one to the other -- did you prefer writing the music over the lyrics, or did you prefer the lyrics, or did you like both?

Well, I tell you -- I preferred the music over the lyrics. But it so happened that I had to get on the other side, too. I didn't dislike it, but I would have preferred writing a tune; I loved to write a tune.
I was thrown into a spot where I had to write lyrics, also.
Right.
So what can you do?
Right. All right, now what do you think -- what, of your favorite song, favorite song - composition, music, that you ever wrote ... what is it? Do you have a favorite?

That's something that I don't know whether anyone really actually knows -- the favorite that they love the most. They'll give you one; they'll say, "Well, I like this one the best" and then a month later, they'd say, "Gee whiz, I shouldn't have said that, I should've said this".
But I don't know of any other tune than a tune called "Traveling All Alone".
I heard you play that at Harmony Hall. That's when I fell in love with you.
Well, that is my favorite tune.
Oh, you did tell me one.
Remember?
I do, I do.
That's my favorite tune.
I want to know why. When you play "One Day" for me, I always cry.
Oh? I don't know, I'll have to play that for you for awhile, I haven't played that for you for a long time.
Uh huh.
And I'd like to play it because that is a beautiful thing if ever there was one --and you recognize beauty, it's the beauty in it that comes, that saturates itself with you.
It's true.

That's all; it just gets under your skin, the beauty of that. To me, I can sit and just play that thing -- I love it, and we love it. I won't say I love it, we love it -- we -- you and I, we both love that tune.
I have so many more questions to ask you, JC, but I think today we'll call it quits and we'll pick up the pieces the next time.
Any time you say.
I think that we could probably go
on talking for about two hours straight, but time is running out for me today.
Right, right.
But I'll be back, and I can't wait.
All right.
And, JC, I thank you.
I will as soon as you come.
And you know, any little old anecdotes that you want to share with all these people at the Smithsonian, you know, we've got to dig up.
Yes, sure.
All right, so long for now.
Thanks a lot.
(END OF REEL ONE)
SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION
Jazz Oral History Project
J.C. Johnson
Reel 2
Interviewed by Surna Rasch (January 1979)
Washington, D.C.
March, 1980

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5395
PROCEEDINGS

MS. RASCH : On the first tape, JC mentioned a song of Irving Berlin's that moved him deeply when he was a kid. The name of this song is "When I Lost You". The second interview with this remarkable man now continues ...
Hi JC, I'm back again.
Oh, fine, glad to have you back -- now we'll get into the nitty gritty, huh?

Right, the nitty gritty. We have a lot to talk about today, and we'll see how it goes. I was thinking that a nice place to begin today would be to talk about the Crescendo Club, and since you were the moving force behind it, I've come to the right person.
Well, I'm glad you came to me. There were about 42 members in that club, and I don't think there are over four around today.
Well, let's see, there's you and there's Eubie Blake. Who were the other couple around?
Walter Bishop.
Uh huh.
And Fred Norman.
Uh huh. How did you start? What was the reason behind your starting this Crescendo Club? It was more than just a club.
Oh sure, it was a real jumping off place for a person who wanted to write, and those who have already written songs, and were eager for a little activity.
Uh huh.
So we organized this group to kind of perpetuate the songs that had already been written.
How did you get together? How did you get that first -- the first big ...
What do they say about something being faster than a telegraph -- word of mouth?
Uh huh.
That's how we did it. Just pass on the word that we had a meeting next Sunday, and pass the word as to where we were going to have it. And like that, we got together.
Do you remember where you first had your first meeting? Have you got any recollection there?
Yes, at Scott Joplin's wife's house.
Uh huh.

That'w where we had our first meeting, and she was very satisfied with having us there. In fact, she was well pleased that we would have our meetings there -- because of him. Lottie Joplin. She was a nice person.
After the meeting, she would always come with
some refreshments, after the meeting was over, she would bring refreshments.
What year was that?
It was '38.
In 1938. You were the first President.
Yes.
And how long were you President?
The entire time the club lasted.
You must have done a good job, JC.
Well, I did the best I could, but we had a lot of fellows -- they were going in all directions at that time; we just couldn't pin them down.
Did we talk about any of the people in the club? Did we name any of them?
No.
Some day we'll go through all the list when we get the letterhead, which I have a copy of.
Sure. That would be swell.
But let's see whom we can recall right now for just a start.
Well, let's see. I can tell you one thing, though. He wasn't a member, but the reason he

wasn't because he lived on the coast, and he wrote two songs that Will Be Here As Long as There Is Time Here - and that was Sheldon Brooks, who wrote "Some of These Days" and "Dark Town Strutters Ball".
Two classics.
Two classics. But he lived out on the west coast, he lived in California.
And there wasn't easy traveling in those there days, was there?
No, no.
That was a haul. Well, I remember seeing Louis Armstrong's name there and Duke Ellington's name and Eubie Blake and W.C. Handy, and this went on in finitum.
Yes, yes.
And we'll maybe take that a part the next time, because right now we want to get started and cover quite a bit of territory.
When you said that you wanted to get together to help perpetuate their music, would you elaborate on that please?

Well, the mostly -- it would be mostly a personal thing, you know -- there was ASCAP. ASCAP -- I call her 'she' -- she doesn't go out and plug songs or anything like that; that's strictly a licensing area. She'd just license the songs to whoever would pay for them, and
then we had songwriters, a society, protective association, and through that organization, you could get a little help in trying to get your songs played by artists.

But to be factual, you had to contact the artist and see if he'd like the song, and play the song for him and he or her -- and see if you could get some consideration that way. That was one of the things that was most important.
You really helped songwriters get in to ASCAP, as a result.
Yes.
Because once you -- you were organized and you had now clout, it wasn't just a person striking out here and there.
Right.
Am I right?
That is absolutely right.
All right. Now, how long did the organization last?
Oh, let's see. We lasted up until the forties, and the next time we talk, I'll have a more accurate forty for you.
Uh huh.
But by organizing the group -- Gene Buck was President of ASCAP at that time, and quite a few members were elected into ASCAP that wouldn't have been

elected, if there had been no organization.
He said the best thing that ever happened was that
you had this organization, and it helped a lot of fellows
that never would have made it here, if they hadn't belonged
to that club.

That's a wonderful contribution.
You've made so many contributions; you made the contribution
on the level of the arts, and then this on the human level,
which is so typical of you, JC.

I love the name, the Crecendo Club, it's got
such dynamism to it. How'd you come up with that name? Was
it you?

Well, it's a musical word. Crecendo
means come up, wow, like that -- that's a crecendo.
Like wow, huh?

Yes. See, when your music is
going and you're directing, and you want to come up with a
crecendo, you bring it right up to a big wham, like that --
that's a crecendo.
A big finish?
Sure.

But it's just so right; I mean
there are lots of musical terms you could have given it.
Well, yeah.
And then, there's also almost a

dual meaning to it because these people are starting together, and they're coming together, and then they're exerting their force and their pressure on society at that swelling again, so the name is just a fine one.
Yes.
Well, tell me -- how did you keep up with the meetings? You know ...

Oh, we only met once a week, on Sundays. Sunday when nobody could squeak about not being able to be there because of the fact that nobody was writing songs on Sunday or trying to dispose of songs on Sunday to publishers.
Right.
So it was a good day to have our meetings.
Did you publish a newsletter? How did you keep people posted; did you have a telephone squad? How did you do that?
Got 42¢ worth of cards -- penny post cards.
(Chuckles)
Penny postcards! Son of a gun, terrific. Now I understand that you also organized another group called the Good Heart Welfare Association.
Yeah, the Good Hearts.
Good Hearts.
Yeah, the Good Hearts.
Would you tell me a bit about that, please?

Yeah, that was just an organization that I thought was necessary at that time, and so I spoke to a lot of people and they thought it was a good idea, so it was just practically, automatically organized to help a lot of people who needed help at that time. I mean, theatrical people, who were really a little bit down on their luck, and we used to give very big, huge affairs at the ballroom in Harlem there, a dance hall. You know the name of it.
Are you talking about ...
The most popular dance hall in Harlem -- oh, what was the name of it?
Gee ... I'm gonna have to fill that in.
Sure, it was the most popular dance hall. So we gave affairs there and we gave affairs at the Renaissance, which is still there, I remember that -- and other little affairs we gave to raise money.
Uh huh. So you ran all these benefits.
Sure.
Did you raise a good sum of money?
So that we could help those who needed help out there.

I think that's wonderful -- artists helping their fellow artists. And I remember reading an article, in fact, that said it was because of the Good Hearts Welfare Association that Mamie Smith got a decent burial. Could you tell us a little about that?

That's correct -- because the people who profited most from Mamie Smith and her success, full days they had nothing to bury her with when she died. And we had taken care of her immediate needs through our association, the Good Hearts, the welfare association, we had taken care of her immediate needs, and when she died, we buried her. And there was no one else to do anything about it; no one came up and said, "Here's $100 toward the burial" that I can remember -- every dime that we used came out of the Treasury.
JC, did Mamie Smith record any of your songs?

Yes, she did. In later years, she recorded songs of mine before, it would have been impossible for her to do when she was with Perry Bradford, because he was sitting in the driver's seat, and anything that she recorded, it would either be his or a part of his. So now that she belonged to our organization, and she wanted to record before she cut out for the green land, why, she recorded a couple of Andy Razaf and my songs.
Uh huh. I understand there was
a tremendous funeral for her, that people converged on the place from all over.

Yes. You're right there. And a funny thing -- those who made the most money with her had nothing to do with her burial. They didn't contribute a dime toward burying Mamie-- we did. The Good Hearts Welfare Association organized, just for the purpose of helping people like Mamie Smith.
You know, it is ironic, but you know, we've talked about it so many times, JC, whatever you give out in life, it comes back to you. A hundred fold.

Now let's talk about your collaborators; you know, all the people you collaborated with -- I'd love to get in to that. And by the way, before we leave Mamie Smith and her records, you told me that you've got some of her original records, and they're jewels, and we'll get together and maybe put a couple of them on the tape when we send this to the Smithsonian. That would be nice.
Fine.
All right. Now, who was the first person you collaborated with?
Andy Razaf.
Uh huh.
He was the first person I collaborated with.
All right, tell us about Andy Razaf
and what was he like, and how did you happen to get together on that first collaboration.

Well, Andy Razaf, I would say, you couldn't get a more talented person than Andy Razaf, because he wrote the song, "Ain't Misbehaving", "Honeysuckle Rose", "Supposing" and oh, so many other songs. Later on. But during his tenure and mine, we wrote an awful lot of songs together, songs that were never published, and never recorded, even. But we wrote them -- we had to have something to do, so we wrote songs.
JC, you have them around, right?
Right.
It might be pretty nice if we got together and made a few contacts and tried to get them published now, or recorded.
Oh, they haven't been published -- it wouldn't mean much at this date, because a published song now doesn't sell unless it's a tremendous hit on record.
Uh huh. I see, that's the way it works.

See, yes, it works that way now. Gee, how times have changed, you know? I remember a time when it took a popular song one year to reach from one coast to the other -- from New York to Los Angeles, it took a year for a song to dribble out there.
And years ago, it was such a struggle for you composers in the beginning; it was blood, sweat and tears ...
Oh, you're telling me.
And today, the composers really are financially rewarded.
Taking over!
They've taken over, right.
Sure, they've taken over. They record their own, they do everything.
Uh huh. Form their own industries.
Sure. Today you're in a whole different field.
It's a far cry from the days of the penny postcards, huh?
Oh, I hope to tell you!
Right. So now you first started with Andy -- do you remember how you first got together? Was it just like a kind of happenstance thing, or what?

Well, we were all in, you might say in the same vicinity, the same neighborhood, you know, you would always gather a spot down in New York there, along about the Brill Building; everybody would be down there running from this publisher to another, trying to place a song with a publisher, and he'd tell you to come back tomorrow, and you'd come back tomorrow, and find out he had gone to Miami, and so
you had to find another place to get the rent money then. So those things were things that happened then. They don't happen now. You can record your own songs.
Right, right.
Now, let's see -- so Andy Razaf and George Whiting -- tell us about your collaboration with them.
Yes, George Whiting -- he was a masterpiece, he was a great lyric writer. Of course, when you write a song like 'My Blue Heaven' you've written something.
That's true.
And that's what he had written when I had met him.
You told me that when you were a kid, that you just dreamed about collaborating with George Whiting some day; you thought it would never be possible.
No, it wasn't him --
Wasn't that George Whiting?
No, no -- George Whiting was -- no.
Who was the collaborator, who was the person that you had ...
Wait a minute, it'll come back to me -- it wasn't George now, because I didn't know anybody from Tin Pan Alley at that time.
No, but when you were young, I thought that you had told me that it was George Whiting.
No, it was someone else.

MS. RASCH: I would like to add now a few words about J. C. Johnson and to quote some of his thoughts and comments. J. C. spent more time in the hospital over the past 12 months than out of the hospital. Many times I visited him when he felt too ill to be taped or was so self conscious about his breathing that he asked to put it on -- put it off, I'm sorry, to the next time.

It's interesting to note, though, that during these times his breathing always seemed to improve as we sat and talked. I did make notes on conversations, however, but I also noticed that, when I would go back to reproduce the information on the tape of things that he'd said freely and easily without a recorder going, he would not elucidate with the recorder on.

From late November, '78, or early December until May, '79, my recorder reel-to-reel remained in his room in New York City. It was frustrating to know the tape recorder was there with which to record, but in deference to the situation or his wishes, could not be used.
Later he went into the hospital, and I picked up my machine, only to discover that some of the taping I thought was on had either not been recording properly at the time or

had been erased. As I said, he's been in and out of the hospital so much. This time he's in the hospital again right now, and he's been there approximately two months. He feels much easier being taped in the hospital via telephone, as he's free to hang up when he gets tired. We will continue to supplement this report with tapes.

In the meantime I would like to share these thoughts that J. C. Johnson shared with me. One of the people that he mentioned was Lew Leslie's Blackbirds in 1932, and the time he referred to this is the beginning of musical comedy. Billy Butler, chairman of the J. C. Johnson Project's artistic committee and a very articulate and well educated man, three degrees from higher institutions, higher education, conducted the orchestra for the Blackbirds, and we know that he will be of great help to the Smithsonian in filling in gaps for their archives, and we'll be in touch with you on his behalf.

J. C. mentioned to me that between 1915 and 1918 he was running an elevator in New York City in the building where Bert Williams either lived or worked. He later mentioned that in the '20s Bert Williams lived at 134th and 7th Avenue. When I asked him what Harlem was like then, he said, 'It was the real Harlem back in the days of Billie Holiday and the Cha-Cha Club on 7th Avenue. It was a wide open village where people used to roam in perfect safety, people of all nationalities.'

He also indicated that Lenox Avenue was the last street to get rid of the trolley. He mentioned Langston Hughes and he and Langston writing something together. J. C. was disappointed about something in Langston and dropped the relationship. He did tell me that Langston initiated it. He still has the papers, the poem and the music in Wortsborough.

During this conversation he made one of his typical J. C. remarks, quote, "Don't let the same bee sting you twice." I found a real absence of ego in J. C. Johnson, and I think it's important to record this. The only time he ever, quote, "blew his own horn," so to speak, was when he mentioned the story of himself and Langston Hughes. And he said, quote, "I was running kind of hot myself when Langston autographed a book and sent it to me. Then he sent me his second book and asked to get together on something." End quote.

Speaking of ego, I got a wonderful insight into J. C. the man when I asked him, "If you started to put your life together for a program, how would you want it to go?" He answered, "It's tough to do that yourself. There's got to be a certain amount of ego, and I always had to reach back and get a little bit of ego out of my back pocket to start up with the other guys."
Once -- another time we were talking about self worth and both of us working on it, and he said, "You've all got it up here. You've paved the way yourself. Be a pacemaker.
You fix it for the next guy. Let him follow you." And interestingly enough, this is what J. C. did do with the Good Hearts Welfare Association and the Crescendo Club.

On April 24th, 1979, a day on which he was lying on bed, lying on the bed totally enervated, washed out, we began talking about music. And he was telling me how he never had to labor over his music. He said that a tune comes into his head and his fingers. Quote, "I can be lying here and a tune will hit me, and I can get up and go to the piano and play what was in my mind before and then elaborate on it. Just that easy, the tune wants out, and the best thing is to let it out."

He also mentioned talks with Gene Buck of ASCAP, et cetera, which I think referred to earlier in the tape. As to Irving Berlin, he said, "Ah, what a wonderful guy. There'll never be another like him. He's the one and only Irving Berlin. I'll never forget the first song he ever wrote, 'When I Lost You'" -- incidentally, we do have reference to this earlier on the tape.

He later mentioned George Whiting being one of the few names to work with Berlin, and they wrote a song, "My Wife's Going to the Country, Hooray, Hooray." I may have mentioned that earlier too. We talked about the turn of the century and the impact of the Wright Brothers. I asked if he could recall his thoughts about them at the time and he said, "I had a feeling" -- this was before they really did -- "I had

a feeling there's a couple of guys that are going to do something. One of these days I'm going to do something, I thought to myself. One of these days I'm going to do something too, and I hope it'll be worthwhile." He emphasized the worthwhile.

I loved it when he talked about his mother. The time he spoke most freely of her was without the tape, and I have my notes on that meeting. "My mother did it all for me," he said, "the one closest to me. I could go to her with anything. I didn't give a hoot. I would tell her everything. She would always know how to deal with it. I'd be so happy just after talking about a situation that affected me, I'd go on and on and feel better." She just sat and let me talk and talk and talk. 'Well,' she'd say, 'you'll work it out.' I wasn't any closer to the solution than when I began talking, but I felt better. And, darn, I did work it out."
What is interesting about this is that J. C. was able to lend an ear to a lot of people and listen to them and let them talk themselves out.

J. C. was pretty reticent about talking about the Mob on tape. But one of the comments that he did make was that the Cotton Club belonged to the Mob and they had it pretty well segregated. He wrote shows for Texas Guynan and in the last two shows Texas Guynan, he mentioned, was ruled by the Mob.

said, quote, "He could get music to talk to him. When he started getting good he'd say, 'talk to me, talk to me, baby.'" Speaking about friends brought a rush of memories. They did not have to know what the problem was or anymore about it and I really appreciate that kind of man."
Commenting on jazz today he said, "Well, jazz today, the endings get to be dragged out. I'm from the old-fashioned school of music and music should end when it's supposed to."

Another thing that J. C. has reiterated time and time again, and that is an ambition to get himself in shape, get to one of those jazz conventions and let them get their say out, especially their incorrect information in history, to stand up and tell them how it really was. And he really rolls the "really."

I asked him how he really got started with music and his answer was, "I always had music, even in the very beginning. My mother sang to me. That's the first thing I remember." His father, by the way, was a chef on the railroads. From the very beginning, music was the most important thing in the universe to J. C., and he has mentioned this several times.

Among the full length shows that he's written, in answer to that question he said, "I began writing full shows in 1927. My first one was a Harlem version of the Zeigfield Follies called 'Desires of 1927.' The next year I wrote, 'Brown Skin Models,' it was moved downtown to Broadway. I wrote through the years, ending up with 'Jazz Train.' We did that show in Europe and it was a Standing Room Only hit in Paris and London."
And then, of course, he talked about the command performance at Windsor Castle before royalty. And I think we have that on the tape in other places.

I asked J. C., what do you think of Bette Midler's recording of your "Empty Bed Blues"? And he said, "It's all right. She's doing it her way. That's the way it's got to be." I thought this was interesting because, of course, Bessie Smith sang that and it made her famous and made him famous. He went on, "An artist has to do it the way they feel it. Would you expect Bessie Smith to do it like Bette Midler? No. As long as artists do it sincerely and in their way. This is their day, now. Then someone else will come along and do it their way. That keeps it going. You want the natural sequence of how they feel. They're not imitating anyone."
And I thought to myself, here is a man so flexible, so open, so unrelated to preconceived ideas, so content not to return to the way it was because he's so well understood
that you can never go back.

In regard to house rent parties in Harlem, on one of the tapes he said, well, they were just what they said they were. And here's some information from him that elucidates it further. He said they got about $10.00 a shot, would make stops at three or four different rent parties on a Saturday night. And they'd make the piano sound like an orchestra, the people would dance to the music. The dances had names like the Bump, the Grind, the Monkey Hunch. A lot of the dances young people are doing today aren't much different, according to J. C.

He said the rent parties really began from old-fashioned church suppers. Members of a congregation would get together in a good-sized railroad flat, have a feast prepared by ladies of the church. There'd be fried chicken, baked ham, pigs feet, gumbo and potato salad. Have I made anybody hungry? It only cost a nominal sum and the money was used to send the pastor on vacation or fix something in the church.
Well, as he said, rents skyrocketed and the idea came to borrow church suppers and raise money to pay the rent.

Some of J. C.'s songs were recorded by the following people: Red Allen, Count Basie, Connie Boswell, Billy Butterfield, Bing Crosby, Duke Ellington, Ella Fitzgerald, Al Hibbler, Earl Hines, Billie Holiday, Claude Hopkins, James P. Johnson,

He has written over 200 songs. I don't know exactly how many are recorded. I think the recording that he's especially proud of is Leonard Bernstein's introduction to music in which he refers to his "Empty Bed Blues" and calls it the greatest blues song ever written. And J. C. is really thrilled with that honor from Leonard Bernstein, and he says, "That's pretty highbrow, isn't it."

J. C. minimizes his own piano playing. His composing is the thing that he's really proud of. But those of us who have sat around and listened to him play the piano feel very, very privileged. He made some tapes of his "Noodling" where he just sits down and composes. It's really an improvisational thing and it's gorgeous. He has this tape at his home in (Wurtzboro), New York, and as soon as he gets out of the hospital again, gets up here, which he does not anticipate until the spring. However, the Smithsonian will get it. He has promised it for them and I know that you'll have it.

In conclusion, I would like to record a statement -- or thoughts, perhaps I should say, about J. C. Johnson, the man. And I would like to say that he's a very special man and a rare human being. His gentlemanliness is as much a part of him as
the color of his eyes, which are blue.

I consider him my contemporary, although he's 83 years old. He wears dignity easily. It naturally becomes him. Yet, he is that fascinating and interesting combination, old world dignity and today's "with it."

I find I can speak to him about anything in the world and I know he will understand. He's a mountain of compassion and understanding. His thoughts flow effortlessly. He is kind. Talking with him is seeing a poet in the original. His mental sensors always find just the right word to catch the right thought. Nothing he says ever sounds prosaic. He's 83 years young; actually, he's ageless.

Being with J. C. to-me is being home. There are not many people with whom I feel totally, absolutely myself. He brings that out in me. I admire him for many reasons, his integrity, his independence, his kindness, and his talent. His talent is only outshone by the man himself. He is part of humankind.

J. C. never looks back. A lot of people who've made it glorify their past. He doesn't have time for that. He wrote a book of poetry when he was 71. He's still revising certain passages. In between his hospital stays he gets to the piano and he plays it and we watch a piano come alive.
He's a humble man who would never compromise values for money. He's his own person. He is one of God's gifts.
And "Perry Winkle" is extremely pleased that the Smithsonian has seen fit to honor J. C. Johnson and include him in their archival history.
(End of proceedings as recorded.)
